carthage.d: A city founded by the Phoenicians, capital of the Punic empire, and later a major Roman city in Africa. A vast archaeological site (the Byrsa Hills, harbors, and thermal baths) listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
carthage.a: Byrsa Hill and its museum; the circular and rectangular Punic harbors; the Antonine Baths by the sea; the Tophet of Salammbô; and the Roman villas of the Odeon.
carthage.c: Plan on spending half a day there and buy the combined ticket, which is valid for all sections, which are spread out over several kilometers.
carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

byrsa.d: A hill that formed the acropolis of Punic Carthage, the site of the citadel, and later the monumental center of Roman Carthage. It is home to the National Museum of Carthage.
byrsa.a: the Punic quarter excavated on the hillside; the National Museum of Carthage; the panoramic view of the ancient harbors and the Gulf of Tunis.
byrsa.c: Head up there in the late morning to catch the light over the bay, then continue on to the nearby Saint-Louis Cathedral.
byrsa.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.
byrsa.leg: According to legend, the Phoenician queen Elissa (Dido), fleeing Tyre, obtained from the Berbers “as much land as an oxhide could cover.” Cleverly, she cut the hide into thin strips to encircle the entire hill: the future Byrsa (“hide” in Greek), the cradle of Carthage. Virgil would make her the tragic lover of Aeneas.

ports puniques de carthage.d: The two ancient ports of Carthage: a rectangular commercial port and a circular military port (the Admiralty Port). Remains that are still visible in the landscape today.
ports puniques de carthage.a: the circular Admiralty island and the body of water in the military port; the rectangular commercial port; the model at the small museum in the Antiquarium.
ports puniques de carthage.c: A site worth a quick visit, best combined with the nearby Tophet.
ports puniques de carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

tophet de carthage.d: The open-air sanctuary of Punic Carthage (the Tophet of Salammbo), where funerary urns and votive stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit were placed.
tophet de carthage.a: the hundreds of votive stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit; the funerary urns lined up in the open-air enclosure.
tophet de carthage.c: A short visit; come early before it gets hot, and combine it with a visit to the nearby Punic ports.
tophet de carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.
tophet de carthage.leg: Sanctuary of Tanit, the great goddess of Carthage. Her symbol—a figure with raised arms—is the precursor to the Hand of Fatima (khamsa), which is found throughout the Mediterranean as a protection against the evil eye. Long portrayed as a site of child sacrifice (an accusation made by Rome and the Bible), the tophet remains a subject of debate among archaeologists.

thermes d'antonin.d: Extensive public baths built in Carthage during the reign of Antoninus Pius, on the seashore. Among the largest baths in the Roman world.
thermes d'antonin.a: The imposing substructures along the waterfront (the vaulted service level that supported the halls), the tall, raised column that conveys the building’s dizzying scale (originally over 30 m high), the frigidarium and the pools, and the view of the Gulf of Tunis.
thermes d'antonin.c: Combine this with the other sites in Carthage (Byrsa and its museum, Roman villas) using the same ticket; come in the morning to enjoy the light and the cool sea breeze—allow about 45 minutes.
thermes d'antonin.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

amphitheatre de carthage.d: An amphitheater from Roman Carthage, largely in ruins, traditionally associated with the martyrdom of Saints Perpetua and Felicity.
amphitheatre de carthage.a: the leveled arena and the commemorative cross marking the martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity; the remains of the bleachers.
amphitheatre de carthage.c: A modest site, best visited as part of a broader tour of the ruins of Carthage.
amphitheatre de carthage.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

citernes de la malga.d: A complex of large Roman cisterns that stored the water brought to Carthage via the Zaghouan Aqueduct.
citernes de la malga.a: The long series of parallel vaulted galleries of the immense Roman reservoir that received water from the Zaghouan aqueduct, some of which have been repurposed as living spaces.
citernes de la malga.c: A quiet, off-the-beaten-path site; worth visiting as a complement to nearby Byrsa.

cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.d: A former Catholic cathedral built in the late 19th century on Byrsa Hill. No longer a place of worship, it now serves as a cultural center (Acropolium).
cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.a: the Neo-Byzantine and Moorish façade; the interior, which has been converted into a cultural space (the Acropolium); the lookout point on Byrsa Hill.
cathedrale saint-louis de carthage.c: Enjoy the view from the terrace right after your visit to the Carthage Museum.

utique (utica).d: An ancient Phoenician city, one of the oldest in North Africa, and later an important Roman city. Remains of houses with mosaics and necropolises. Today it is located about 10 km from the sea (due to silting of the Medjerda Delta).
utique (utica).a: the House of the Waterfall and its mosaics, still in place; the ruins of the thermal baths; the small museum displaying Punic sarcophagi and pottery.
utique (utica).c: A quiet, off-the-beaten-path spot; be sure to combine your visit with a stop at the Utique Museum on site.
utique (utica).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

kerkouane.d: A Punic city abandoned around the 3rd century B.C. and never rebuilt, it is a rare example of Phoenician-Punic urban planning. It is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
kerkouane.a: the complete map of the Punic city, showing its streets and houses; the pink bathtubs in the private baths; the small museum and the rock-cut necropolis.
kerkouane.c: The only surviving purely Punic city; best visited in conjunction with the Cap Bon coast and Kelibia.
kerkouane.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

necropole de kerkouane.d: A rock-cut necropolis associated with the Punic city of Kerkouane, featuring tombs carved into the rock.
necropole de kerkouane.a: Punic tombs carved into the rock, serving as a burial site for the neighboring city of Kerkouane.
necropole de kerkouane.c: Be sure to check this out while you're visiting the Kerkouane site, to which it belongs.

dougga (thugga).d: An ancient city of Numidian and later Roman origin, it is one of the best-preserved ancient sites in North Africa (Capitol, theater, temples, Libyco-Punic mausoleum). It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
dougga (thugga).a: the Capitol with its Corinthian columns; the theater nestled against the hill; the Libyan-Punic mausoleum; the Place des Vents; and the latrines with twelve seats.
dougga (thugga).c: Extensive ruins on a slope: hiking shoes and at least two hours; magnificent in the low morning sun.
dougga (thugga).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.
dougga (thugga).an: The best-preserved ancient city in North Africa. Look for the Libyco-Punic mausoleum: its bilingual inscription (Punic and Libyan) made it possible to decipher the Libyan alphabet, the ancestor of the Berber Tifinagh script.

capitole de dougga.d: The Thugga Capitol, dedicated to the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva), was built in the 2nd century. Its columned façade is one of the site’s most iconic monuments.
capitole de dougga.a: the tall façade with six Corinthian columns and its sculpted pediment; the podium overlooking the forum.
capitole de dougga.c: An iconic landmark of the site; best photographed early in the day to avoid backlighting.
capitole de dougga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

theatre de dougga.d: The Roman theater in Thugga, built in the 2nd century, is set against a hillside and well-preserved; it is still used for performances.
theatre de dougga.a: the well-preserved bleachers, which seat about 3,500 spectators; the stage and the view of the Khalled Wadi plain.
theatre de dougga.c: Sit at the top of the bleachers to enjoy the view; it's still used in the summer for shows.
theatre de dougga.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).d: A large Roman amphitheater from ancient Thysdrus, dating from the 3rd century, and one of the best-preserved in the world. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).a: the stacked arches on the facade; the arena and the underground passages where animals and gladiators moved about; the climbable bleachers.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).c: Head up to the upper levels for the view; combine this with a visit to the El Jem Museum and its mosaics.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).leg: Legend links this arena to El Kahena, the Berber warrior queen who is said to have resisted the Arab conquerors; there are even said to be underground passages connecting the amphitheater to the coast.
amphitheatre d'el jem (thysdrus).an: The third-largest Roman amphitheater in the world (~35,000 seats), located in a small town: it’s almost as big as the Colosseum. It served as a filming location for the movie *Gladiator*. Climb up the stands and descend into the underground chambers where the wild beasts were kept.

sbeitla (sufetula).d: An ancient Roman and Byzantine city notable for its forum and its three adjacent Capitoline temples, as well as its Christian basilicas.
sbeitla (sufetula).a: The Sufetula Forum, which opens onto three adjacent Capitoline temples dedicated to the Triad, the Arch of Antoninus Pius, and several Christian basilicas with baptisteries.
sbeitla (sufetula).c: Plan on spending 2 to 3 hours on the tour, and take advantage of the low-angle light in the morning or late afternoon to photograph the capitols.
sbeitla (sufetula).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

capitole de sbeitla.d: An exceptional complex of three distinct Capitoline temples dedicated to the triad, opening onto the Forum of Sufetula.
capitole de sbeitla.a: The three distinct and well-preserved Capitoline temples, aligned behind the arch and the forum—a rare example of a triad of separate buildings.
capitole de sbeitla.c: Combine this with the rest of the Sufetula site right nearby; this highlight only takes a few minutes to see.
capitole de sbeitla.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

bulla regia.d: A Roman city known for its villas with underground floors designed to provide relief from the heat, adorned with mosaics still in place (House of the Hunt, House of Amphitrite).
bulla regia.a: the villas with underground levels (the House of the Hunt, the House of Amphitrite) with their mosaics still in place; the theater and the baths of Julia Memmia.
bulla regia.c: Go down into the underground houses, which stay cool even in the middle of summer; mosaics can be seen in situ.
bulla regia.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.
bulla regia.an: To escape the heat wave, wealthy Romans built underground villas there—an entire floor below ground, cool and with mosaics still intact. Go down and see the House of Amphitrite.

thuburbo majus.d: A prosperous Roman city in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, featuring a forum, a Capitol, temples, and thermal baths (winter and summer) that are still visible today.
thuburbo majus.a: the Capitol standing on its podium; the paved forum; the winter and summer baths; and the Petronii Gymnasium.
thuburbo majus.c: A peaceful, rolling landscape, best enjoyed in combination with the nearby Zaghouan Temple of Waters.
thuburbo majus.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

makthar (mactaris).d: An ancient city of Numidian origin that later became Roman, featuring Trajan's Arch, the Great Southern Baths, and the "House of Venus." Located at a high elevation in the high steppe.
makthar (mactaris).a: Trajan's Arch, the well-preserved Great Southern Baths, the "House of Venus," and the Schola of the Juvenes, set against the backdrop of the high steppe.
makthar (mactaris).c: Be sure to bring water and sturdy shoes, as the site is large and exposed; the tour takes about 2 hours and is pleasant in the spring.
makthar (mactaris).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

chemtou (simitthus).d: An ancient site famous for its quarries of Numidian yellow marble (marmor numidicum), which were exploited by the Romans, featuring a Roman bridge, a theater, and a basilica.
chemtou (simitthus).a: the Numidian yellow marble quarries; the Roman bridge over the Medjerda River; the theater, the basilica, and the excellent marble museum.
chemtou (simitthus).c: Don't miss the modern museum that explains how the famous ancient marble was quarried.
chemtou (simitthus).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

pont de trajan (chemtou).d: A Roman bridge spanning the Medjerda River near Simitthus, associated with the quarrying and transport of marble from Chemtou.
pont de trajan (chemtou).a: The remains of the Roman bridge spanning the Medjerda Wadi, which was used to transport marble from Chemtou.
pont de trajan (chemtou).c: A brief stop during the tour of the Chemtou site; the wadi is shallower and easier to cross outside the rainy season.

oudhna (uthina).d: A Roman colony south of Tunis, featuring an amphitheater, a capitol, thermal baths, and cisterns. It also has a significant villa and mosaics.
oudhna (uthina).a: the partially restored amphitheater; the Capitol and its cisterns; the ruins of villas with mosaics.
oudhna (uthina).c: Near Tunis, ideal for a half-day trip combined with Thuburbo Majus.
oudhna (uthina).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

haidra (ammaedara).d: A former Roman and later Byzantine city near the Algerian border, featuring a vast Byzantine fortress, arches, and Christian basilicas.
haidra (ammaedara).a: The vast Byzantine fortress with its imposing ramparts, triumphal arches, the Church of Melleus, and several Christian basilicas near the Algerian border.
haidra (ammaedara).c: This is a remote and isolated location: bring water, allow 2 hours, and check for directions before you go.
haidra (ammaedara).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

gightis (gigthis).d: A former Punic trading post and later a Roman city on the Gulf of Bou Ghrara, featuring a forum, a capitol, thermal baths, and temples.
gightis (gigthis).a: Remains of a Punic and later Roman city on the Gulf of Bou Ghrara: a paved forum, the Capitol, thermal baths, and temple foundations.
gightis (gigthis).c: The site is open during the day and has little shade: be sure to bring water and a hat, and check the AMVPPC schedule on site.
gightis (gigthis).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

pupput.d: A Roman city on the coast near Hammamet, known for its necropolis and the mosaics found in its houses.
pupput.a: Remains of a Roman coastal city near Hammamet: a necropolis and mosaics from residential buildings.
pupput.c: A modest, off-the-beaten-path site in the South Hammamet hotel zone; a quick visit worth combining with a tour of the Hammamet medina.
pupput.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

hadrumete (hadrumetum, sousse antique).d: A former Phoenician settlement that became a major Roman city (Hadrumetum), located beneath present-day Sousse. Christian catacombs and rich mosaics.
hadrumete (hadrumetum, sousse antique).a: Layers of ancient Hadrumetum beneath modern-day Sousse: a Punic and then Roman legacy, which gave rise to the Christian catacombs and the mosaics on display at the museum.
hadrumete (hadrumetum, sousse antique).c: Since the ruins are scattered throughout the modern city, the Kasbah Archaeological Museum offers the best overview.

catacombes de sousse.d: An extensive network of early Christian burial galleries carved beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs.
catacombes de sousse.a: An extensive network of early Christian burial galleries carved beneath ancient Hadrumetum, containing thousands of tombs; only a portion of it is open to visitors.
catacombes de sousse.c: Check on site to make sure the open section is accessible, as access to the catacombs is sometimes restricted.
catacombes de sousse.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

neapolis (nabeul).d: An ancient coastal city near present-day Nabeul, known for its garum production workshops and a large house with mosaics.
neapolis (nabeul).a: Ancient garum production workshops by the sea and a large house with mosaics, evidence of the activity in the coastal city of Neapolis.
neapolis (nabeul).c: An outdoor site near the Nabeul waterfront, best visited in conjunction with the city's archaeological museum.

thuburnica.d: A Roman city in northwestern Tunisia, featuring a Roman bridge believed to date from the time of Trajan and various other ruins.
thuburnica.a: The Roman bridge, believed to date from the time of Trajan, which is still standing, and various scattered ruins of the ancient city in the middle of the countryside.
thuburnica.c: A small, secluded rural town: be sure to bring a car and sturdy shoes; combine this visit with a trip to nearby Chemtou.

musti (mustis).d: A Roman city on the Carthage–Theveste road, featuring temples, the Arch of Gordian III, and oil mills. Coordinates of the site's center.
musti (mustis).a: The temples, the Arch of Gordian III, the macellum, and the ancient oil mills lining the Carthage-Theveste road.
musti (mustis).c: An easy roadside stop that takes about an hour to explore; can be combined with a visit to El Krib.

sicca veneria (le kef antique).d: An ancient Numidian and later Roman city located beneath the modern city of El Kef, known for its sanctuary and ancient cisterns.
sicca veneria (le kef antique).a: The ancient ruins visible just below the surface of the modern city, including Roman cisterns and traces of the sanctuary of Venus.
sicca veneria (le kef antique).c: Explore the medina of El Kef, which covers the ancient city, as you stroll through it.

cillium (kasserine).d: A Roman city near Kasserine, featuring a theater, an arch, and the Flavian Mausoleum. Approximate coordinates of the ancient site.
cillium (kasserine).a: The theater, the arch, and especially the three-story Flavian Mausoleum, an ancient site on the outskirts of Kasserine.
cillium (kasserine).c: Approximate coordinates of the area: First, locate the Mausoleum of the Flavii, which is the most prominent landmark.

bataille de zama (emplacement presume).d: Site of Scipio Africanus's victory over Hannibal, marking the end of the Second Punic War. The exact location remains a matter of debate; presumed coordinates (Wikidata), to be considered approximate.
bataille de zama (emplacement presume).a: There are no ruins to see: this is a memorial to Scipio's victory over Hannibal (202 B.C.), the exact location of which remains a matter of debate.
bataille de zama (emplacement presume).c: A site of purely historical interest; the real appeal lies in the ancient cities nearby (Zama Regia, Naraggara).

medina de tunis.d: The historic heart of Tunis, founded in the 7th–9th centuries, featuring a dense network of souks, mosques, and palaces. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
medina de tunis.a: the Zitouna Mosque; the covered souks (perfume shops, chechias); the Dar Hussein and Dar Lasram palaces; the Bab Bhar and Bab Jedid gates; the panoramic terraces of the cafés.
medina de tunis.c: Lose yourself in the morning when the souks come to life; head up to a café terrace for a view of the minarets.

mosquee zitouna (grande mosquee de tunis.d: The Grand Mosque, the main religious monument in the medina of Tunis, was founded during the Umayyad/Aghlabid period and served as a center of learning for many years.
mosquee zitouna (grande mosquee de tunis.a: the large prayer hall with its reused ancient columns; the vast paved courtyard and its sundial; the minaret.
mosquee zitouna (grande mosquee de tunis.c: Modest attire is required; the courtyard is open to non-Muslim visitors during the day.
mosquee zitouna (grande mosquee de tunis.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

mosquee sidi mahrez (tunis).d: An Ottoman-era mosque in the Medina of Tunis, notable for its Ottoman-inspired domes, dedicated to the city's patron saint.
mosquee sidi mahrez (tunis).a: the cluster of white domes inspired by the Ottoman style of Istanbul, unique to Tunis; the zaouïa of the patron saint across the street.
mosquee sidi mahrez (tunis).c: A striking silhouette visible from the narrow streets of the Bab Souika neighborhood.
mosquee sidi mahrez (tunis).leg: Sidi Mahrez (10th century) is the patron saint of Tunis, “the sultan of the medina”: tradition credits him with rebuilding and protecting the city. His mosque, with its white domes and Ottoman-style architecture, pays homage to him.

grande mosquee de kairouan.d: The Great Mosque of Kairouan (Oqba ibn Nafi Mosque), one of the oldest and most important religious complexes in the Muslim West, was founded in the 7th century.
grande mosquee de kairouan.a: the vast courtyard and its sundial; the massive three-story minaret; the prayer hall with its reused columns and mihrab adorned with glazed tiles.
grande mosquee de kairouan.c: Appropriate attire is required; the courtyard is open to visitors, and the prayer hall can be seen from the doorway.
grande mosquee de kairouan.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.
grande mosquee de kairouan.leg: The first holy city of Islam in the Maghreb (670), founded by Okba Ibn Nafi. Legend has it that a spring gushed forth where his horse struck the ground, revealing a golden cup lost in Mecca. It is said that seven pilgrimages to Kairouan are worth one hajj.

raqqada.d: Former princely residence and Aghlabid capital south of Kairouan. Site of the National Museum of Islamic Art.
raqqada.a: Former Aghlabid princely capital south of Kairouan, now best known for its National Museum of Islamic Art (Kairouan Quranic manuscripts).
raqqada.c: The site is far from the city center: combine your visit with a trip to Kairouan by car.

al-mansuriya (sabra).d: A former Fatimid and later Zirid palace city near Kairouan, now largely in ruins. Approximate coordinates of the site.
al-mansuriya (sabra).a: Heavily eroded remains of a Fatimid and later Zirid palatial city, now largely gone; of primarily archaeological interest.
al-mansuriya (sabra).c: A poorly organized and difficult-to-navigate site: best suited for archaeology enthusiasts, ideally accompanied by a guide.

medina de sousse.d: The fortified medina of Sousse, with its ramparts, kasbah, ribat, and grand mosque. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
medina de sousse.a: the crenellated ramparts; the ribat and its watchtower; the kasbah, home to the museum and its mosaics; the Great Mosque.
medina de sousse.c: Climb up to the Ribat Tower or the Kasbah for a view of the medina and the harbor.

ribat de sousse.d: The Ribat (fortress-monastery) of Sousse, built during the Aghlabid period (8th–9th centuries), with its watchtower (nador) overlooking the medina.
ribat de sousse.a: the fortified courtyard and the cells of the soldier-monks; the oratory; the watchtower (nador), which offers a panoramic view of the medina.
ribat de sousse.c: Climb the narrow tower early in the morning to catch the light and avoid the crowds.
ribat de sousse.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

grande mosquee de sousse.d: The 9th-century Great Mosque of Sousse, with its simple, fortified design, is located in the heart of the medina near the ribat.
grande mosquee de sousse.a: the courtyard lined with galleries; the corner turrets reminiscent of a fortress; the austere Aghlabid prayer hall.
grande mosquee de sousse.c: Just a stone's throw from the ribat—a must-see on the same tour of the medina.
grande mosquee de sousse.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

ribat de monastir.d: The Ribat of Monastir, one of the oldest Islamic defensive structures in Ifriqiya (founded around 796), was expanded over the centuries.
ribat de monastir.a: the maze of courtyards, rooms, and staircases; the panoramic watchtower; the museum of Islamic art located within the complex.
ribat de monastir.c: A setting for famous films; climb the tower for a view of the sea and the Bourguiba Mausoleum.
ribat de monastir.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

grande mosquee de monastir.d: The Great Mosque of Monastir, located next to the ribat, dates back to the Middle Ages and has been renovated several times.
grande mosquee de monastir.a: A mosque dating back to the Middle Ages that has been remodeled several times, located right next to the ribat.
grande mosquee de monastir.c: Follow this up with a visit to the nearby ribat; appropriate attire is required.
grande mosquee de monastir.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

mahdia (medina et site historique).d: The former Fatimid capital, founded in the 10th century on a fortified peninsula, with its monumental gate (Skifa Kahla) and its grand mosque.
mahdia (medina et site historique).a: the monumental Skifa Kahla Gate; the reconstructed Fatimid Grand Mosque; the Borj el-Kebir; the maritime cemetery; and Cape Africa.
mahdia (medina et site historique).c: Take a stroll around the peninsula at sunset; the fishing port comes to life early in the morning.

grande mosquee de mahdia.d: The Great Fatimid Mosque of Mahdia, rebuilt in the 20th century to match the original 10th-century design.
grande mosquee de mahdia.a: the monumental portico façade and its projecting gateway, a reconstruction of the 10th-century Fatimid design; the courtyard opening onto the sea.
grande mosquee de mahdia.c: Beautiful late-afternoon light on the light-colored stone, facing the harbor.
grande mosquee de mahdia.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

grande mosquee de sfax.d: The Great Mosque in the heart of the Sfax medina, founded during the Aghlabid period (9th century) and expanded several times.
grande mosquee de sfax.a: the minaret with its carved geometric decorations; the facades adorned with inscriptions; its location in the heart of the medina's souks.
grande mosquee de sfax.c: Walk around the minaret through the narrow streets of the souks to take in the scenery.
grande mosquee de sfax.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

grande mosquee de testour.d: Testour Mosque, in a town founded in the 17th century by Andalusians (Moriscos) who had been expelled from Spain; the minaret features Hispano-Moorish influences and includes a clock.
grande mosquee de testour.a: the Hispano-Moorish minaret with a clock; the Andalusian architectural elements introduced by the Moriscos; the town square, founded in the 17th century.
grande mosquee de testour.c: Combine it with the summer malouf festival; a picturesque Andalusian village on the Medjerda River.
grande mosquee de testour.h: Place of worship — open to visitors during business hours; appropriate attire required.

le kef (kasbah et medina).d: A hilltop city in the northwest, dominated by its Ottoman kasbah, built atop the ancient Sicca Veneria. A complex of mosques, zaouias, and a basilica.
le kef (kasbah et medina).a: The Ottoman kasbah overlooking the city, the medina with its mosques and zaouias, and the early Christian basilica Dar El Kous, all superimposed on the ancient Sicca Veneria.
le kef (kasbah et medina).c: A charming town that's pleasant to explore on foot; plan on spending half a day there and be sure to wear sturdy shoes for the sloping alleys.

basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.d: An ancient Christian basilica (known as Dar El Kous) in El Kef, one of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia.
basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.a: One of the best-preserved early Christian buildings in Tunisia, with its apse and arches still intact.
basilique saint-pierre (dar el kous, le.c: A short visit to the heart of El Kef, to be included as part of a tour of the medina.

synagogue de la ghriba (djerba).d: The oldest synagogue in Tunisia, located in Erriadh (Hara Seghira) on the island of Djerba, is the site of an annual Jewish pilgrimage.
synagogue de la ghriba (djerba).a: The oldest synagogue in Tunisia, located in Erriadh, has an interior lined with earthenware tiles and is the site of an annual Jewish pilgrimage.
synagogue de la ghriba (djerba).c: Appropriate attire is required; crowds are at their peak during the spring pilgrimage (Lag Ba'omer).
synagogue de la ghriba (djerba).leg: The oldest synagogue in Africa. Tradition has it that a stone fell from the sky to mark its location, and that a mysterious young girl, *la Ghriba* (“the stranger”), lived there alone—found unharmed after a fire. One of the doors is said to have come from the Temple in Jerusalem. The pilgrimage is still alive today.

mosquee de djerba (architecture djerbien.d: A traditional mosque in the Djerba architectural style, featuring whitewashed walls and domes characteristic of the island.
mosquee de djerba (architecture djerbien.a: Typical Djerba architecture: whitewashed structures, rounded domes, and clean lines.
mosquee de djerba (architecture djerbien.c: Access to the interior may be restricted to the faithful; be sure to admire the white spaces bathed in low-angled light.

meninx.d: The main ancient city on the island of Djerba, renowned in antiquity for its production of purple dye. Ruins of a forum and an amphitheater.
meninx.a: The main ancient city of Djerba, once famous for its purple dye: ruins of a forum and remnants of buildings in the southern part of the island.
meninx.c: An open-air archaeological site with minimal facilities: closed-toe shoes and water are recommended.

ksar ouled soltane.d: A Berber ksar with ghorfas (multi-story storage cells) south of Tataouine, among the best-preserved in southern Tunisia.
ksar ouled soltane.a: One of the best-preserved ksour a ghorfas in the south, with its storage cells stacked several stories high around courtyards.
ksar ouled soltane.c: The light and photo opportunities are best in the late afternoon; the site is managed by the AMVPPC; check the hours on site.
ksar ouled soltane.h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

chenini (ksar et village).d: A hilltop Berber village in the Tataouine region, built around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries.
chenini (ksar et village).a: A Berber village perched around a ridge-top ksar and fortified granaries, with its white mosque below.
chenini (ksar et village).c: Hike on a rocky trail: wear sturdy shoes and go early in the morning to avoid the heat.

douiret (ksar et village).d: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, southwest of Tataouine, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.
douiret (ksar et village).a: A Berber cave village and its hilltop ksar, long inhabited by an Amazigh community.
douiret (ksar et village).c: The terrain is steep and exposed: be sure to bring water, a hat, and hiking shoes.

guermessa (ksar et village).d: A hilltop Berber village with a ksar perched on a ridge, in the Tataouine region, less crowded than Chenini and Douiret.
guermessa (ksar et village).a: A hilltop Berber village with a ksar on the ridge, quieter and less crowded than Chenini and Douiret.
guermessa (ksar et village).c: Access can be difficult at times: a 4x4 or a local guide makes the climb easier.

ksar hadada.d: Ksar a Ghorfas, north of Tataouine (Ghomrassen region), partially restored.
ksar hadada.a: A partially restored ksar a ghorfas, north of Tataouine near Ghomrassen.
ksar hadada.c: A quick visit is possible; this can be combined with a tour of the neighboring ksour in the Ghomrassen region.

ksar hallouf.d: A fortified ksar in the Medenine region (Beni Khedache) stands on a hill overlooking the valley.
ksar hallouf.a: A fortified ksar stands on a hill overlooking the valley in the Beni Khedache region.
ksar hallouf.c: Mountain Roads: Drive Carefully and Stay Hydrated in the Heat.

matmata.d: A Berber village known for its cave dwellings carved into a crater in the ground. Coordinates of the village center.
matmata.a: A village known for its cave dwellings, which are carved into the ground in a crater-like formation around circular courtyards.
matmata.c: Some houses are open to visitors; please respect the residents' privacy and avoid visiting during the hottest part of the day.
matmata.an: The troglodyte houses in the crater served as Luke Skywalker's home in *Star Wars*: the planet Tatooine owes its name to the nearby town of Tataouine. The Sidi Driss Hotel is still open to visitors.

toujane.d: A Berber mountain village clinging to the slopes of the Matmata Mountains, renowned for its weaving and terraced landscape.
toujane.a: A Berber village nestled on the slopes of the Matmata Mountains, renowned for its weaving and terraced fields.
toujane.c: The scenic route from Matmata is beautiful: drive slowly to enjoy the views.

takrouna.d: A Berber village perched on a rocky outcrop near Enfidha, with its ancient, whitewashed buildings. Approximate coordinates of the village's highest point.
takrouna.a: the old white village perched on its rocky outcrop; the zaouïa at the summit; the 360° view of the Sahel plain.
takrouna.c: Head to the top for the view; there's a café overlooking the village.

salakta (sullecthum).d: An ancient Roman port in the Sahel (Sullecthum), a center for the production and export of olive oil and garum. A small museum and coastal ruins.
salakta (sullecthum).a: An ancient Roman port in the Sahel, a center for the production of oil and garum: coastal ruins and a small local museum (lion mosaic).
salakta (sullecthum).c: Combine a visit to the site and its museum, and enjoy the waterfront.

thaenae (thyna).d: A Roman city south of Sfax, at the far end of the Fossa Regia, featuring thermal baths, basilicas, and mosaics.
thaenae (thyna).a: A Roman city south of Sfax, at the far end of the Fossa Regia: ruins of thermal baths, basilicas, and mosaics.
thaenae (thyna).c: A large, mostly unshaded site right on the beach: be sure to bring water and sturdy shoes.

temple des eaux de zaghouan.d: A monumental nymphaeum stands at the foot of Djebel Zaghouan, capturing the springs that fed the Carthage aqueduct.
temple des eaux de zaghouan.a: The Roman nymphaeum, built in a semicircular shape against the side of the djebel, with its basin and niches that captured the springs feeding the Carthage aqueduct, set amid wooded surroundings.
temple des eaux de zaghouan.c: Above the town of Zaghouan; a lovely, cool stop—perfect to combine with a hike up to the national park.

limes tripolitanus (frontiere saharienne.d: A system of fortifications and trails controlling the southern border of Roman Africa (outposts, small forts, centenaria) in the pre-Saharan region. Approximate coordinates for a sector.
limes tripolitanus (frontiere saharienne.a: A network of Roman forts, outposts, and trails controlling the Saharan border; scattered ruins in the pre-Saharan region.
limes tripolitanus (frontiere saharienne.c: Wide-open, desert-like terrain: A 4x4 vehicle, a guide, and a supply of water are essential.

tisavar (ksar rhilane).d: A Roman fort (centenarium) on the Limes Tripolitanus, standing alone on the edge of the desert near Ksar Ghilane.
tisavar (ksar rhilane).a: A Roman fort (centenarium) on the Limes, standing alone on the edge of the desert near Ksar Ghilane.
tisavar (ksar rhilane).c: Access via the Saharan trail: 4x4 vehicle and guide recommended; bring water.
tisavar (ksar rhilane).h: Site managed by the AMVPPC — open during the day; hours vary by season; please check on site.

grande mosquee de gafsa.d: The Great Mosque of Gafsa, located in the heart of the oasis, near the city's Roman pools. This region is known for its prehistoric Capsian culture.
grande mosquee de gafsa.a: The Great Mosque in the heart of the Gafsa oasis, just a stone's throw from the Roman pools.
grande mosquee de gafsa.c: The interior is often reserved for worshippers; combine your visit with a tour of the nearby medina.

gisement prehistorique d'el mekta (capsi.d: A site of the same name and a key reference point for Capsian (Epipaleolithic) culture near Gafsa, featuring snail shells and stone tool technology. Coordinates of the site.
gisement prehistorique d'el mekta (capsi.a: A site named after the Capsian culture: snail shell mounds and Epipaleolithic stone tool production.
gisement prehistorique d'el mekta (capsi.c: A site of primarily scientific interest, not particularly spectacular: a guide or the Gafsa Museum can help you understand it.

piscines romaines de gafsa.d: Roman pools fed by springs in the heart of the medina of Gafsa, ancient Capsa. Two central open-air pools bearing Latin inscriptions.
piscines romaines de gafsa.a: Two open-air Roman pools fed by springs, featuring Latin inscriptions, in the heart of the medina.
piscines romaines de gafsa.c: A short tour with some shaded areas; combine it with a visit to the nearby museum and mosque.

hammam mellegue (thermes romains).d: Ancient Roman baths that are still in use, located on the Mellegue River about 10 km southwest of El Kef. The original pools and structures are still fed by thermal waters.
hammam mellegue (thermes romains).a: Roman baths still fed by thermal waters, with ancient pools and structures still in use, on the banks of the Mellegue wadi.
hammam mellegue (thermes romains).c: Access is via a dirt road about 10 km southwest of El Kef: be sure to use a suitable vehicle and check the road conditions.

kasbah du kef.d: The Ottoman fortress of Kef, built beginning in 1600 to defend and administer the city. It overlooks the medina and now hosts cultural events.
kasbah du kef.a: The Ottoman fortress (built in 1600) overlooking the medina, with its ramparts and bastions, now serves as a venue for cultural events.
kasbah du kef.c: Go up in the late afternoon to enjoy the view of the city and the plain; allow about 1 hour.

zaouia de sidi bou makhlouf.d: A zaouia housing the tomb of Sidi Bou Makhlouf, the patron saint of El Kef, at the foot of the Kasbah ramparts (dating from the 17th century), featuring domes and an octagonal minaret. Approximate coordinates.
zaouia de sidi bou makhlouf.a: The mausoleum of the patron saint of El Kef, with its domes and octagonal minaret, at the foot of the kasbah’s ramparts.
zaouia de sidi bou makhlouf.c: A short visit, followed by a climb up to the nearby kasbah.

synagogue de la ghriba du kef.d: Former synagogue in the Jewish quarter of La Hara, known as Ghribet el Kef, of the Sephardic rite. Abandoned in 1984, then restored and reopened in 1994.
synagogue de la ghriba du kef.a: The former Sephardic synagogue in the Jewish quarter of La Hara, restored and reopened in 1994.
synagogue de la ghriba du kef.c: A small building worth seeing while strolling through the medina; access may sometimes require a local permit.

musee regional des arts et traditions du.d: An ethnographic museum housed in the former zaouïa of Sidi Ben Aissa, a Sufi complex dating from 1784. Opened in 1970, it showcases the way of life of Tunisia's tribes.
musee regional des arts et traditions du.a: Ethnographic collections on the way of life of the tribes of Tunisia, in the former Sufi zaouia of Sidi Ben Aissa (1784).
musee regional des arts et traditions du.c: Allow about 1 hour; this is a great way to get a feel for the local culture before exploring the region.
musee regional des arts et traditions du.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.

thignica (ain tounga).d: An ancient city in the Medjerda Valley, near Testour and Dougga. Notable ruins of a Byzantine fortress, temples, thermal baths, and dwellings.
thignica (ain tounga).a: The prominent Byzantine fortress that overlooks the site, as well as the ruins of Roman temples, baths, and dwellings in the Medjerda Valley.
thignica (ain tounga).c: A quick stop on the road from Testour to Dougga; wear walking shoes to approach the fortress.

thibaris (thibar).d: An ancient Roman city built on the site of a colony of Marius’s veterans, which later became a municipality. It featured a basilica and an amphitheater; a Christian bishopric is attested as early as 256.
thibaris (thibar).a: The ruins of the basilica and amphitheater of the ancient Roman colony, set in a rural landscape.
thibaris (thibar).c: A small, unassuming site: a brief stop is enough, best combined with visits to the other ancient cities in the Medjerda Valley.

uchi maius (henchir-ed-douames).d: A Numidian city that came under Roman control after the Jugurthine War; it became a colony under Alexander Severus. The Arch of Alexander Severus, the Arch of Gordian III, the forum, the baths, and the basilica.
uchi maius (henchir-ed-douames).a: The Arch of Severus Alexander and the Arch of Gordian III, the forum, the baths, and the basilica of this Numidian-Roman city near Dougga.
uchi maius (henchir-ed-douames).c: This site is off the main roads: plan to hire a guide or arrange for a suitable vehicle, and combine this visit with a trip to Dougga.

numluli (henchir el matria).d: A Roman city covering approximately 18 ha between Beja and Dougga, one of the best-preserved sites in the north. It features a forum with a capitol, two thermal baths, an early Christian basilica, and cisterns.
numluli (henchir el matria).a: The forum with its capitol, two sets of thermal baths, an early Christian basilica, and cisterns, in one of the best-preserved cities in the north, between Béja and Dougga.
numluli (henchir el matria).c: A rural, off-the-beaten-path site: plan to bring a vehicle and water, and combine this visit with Dougga as part of the same trip.

agbia (ain hedja).d: A Numidian and later Roman city (Municipium Agbiensium) near Dougga. A late Byzantine stronghold on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road.
agbia (ain hedja).a: The late Byzantine fort, situated on a hill overlooking the ancient Roman road, and the scattered ruins of the Numidian-Roman city.
agbia (ain hedja).c: A short hike near Dougga; the climb is brief, but be sure to wear sturdy shoes.

thunusuda (sidi-meskin).d: A city known as Africa Proconsularis in the Medjerda Valley, between Chemtou and Bulla Regia, near Bou Salem. An ancient episcopal see.
thunusuda (sidi-meskin).a: The scattered ruins of this ancient city in the Medjerda Valley, a former episcopal see, located between Chemtou and Bulla Regia.
thunusuda (sidi-meskin).c: A modest, sparsely developed site near Bou Salem: a quick stop to combine with the major nearby attractions.

althiburos (el medeina).d: A Numidian and later Roman city in the Dahmani district (Le Kef), one of the oldest known Numidian settlements. It features a forum, temples, a theater, an arch, and houses with mosaics.
althiburos (el medeina).a: The forum, temples, theater, arch, and mosaic-adorned residences of one of the oldest known Numidian settlements.
althiburos (el medeina).c: Near Dahmani; be sure to bring water and allow about 1 hour and 30 minutes to explore this sprawling, largely undeveloped site.

assuras (henchir zanfour).d: A Roman city in Proconsular Africa, located between Siliana and the Sers. It featured temples, a theater, and Augustan mausoleums; it served as a bishopric from the mid-3rd century onward.
assuras (henchir zanfour).a: The temples, theater, and Augustan mausoleums of this Roman city, which later became a bishopric.
assuras (henchir zanfour).c: A rural location between Siliana and Le Sers, with few signs: a guide or precise coordinates will help you find it.

chusira (kesra).d: An ancient city located beneath Kesra, Tunisia’s highest Berber village, near Makthar. The Numidian city of Thusca, a bishopric.
chusira (kesra).a: The ancient ruins of Numidian Thusca, located in Kesra—Tunisia’s highest Berber village, with its terraced stone houses.
chusira (kesra).c: The hilltop village is just as worth seeing as the ruins; combine your visit with a trip to nearby Makthar and enjoy the panoramic views.

zama regia (jama).d: A Numidian city near Jama, which later became a Roman colony. Its location was confirmed by an inscription in 2002; the temple features numerous sculptures.
zama regia (jama).a: The ruins of the Numidian city that became a Roman colony, including a temple with numerous sculptures; its location was confirmed by an inscription in 2002.
zama regia (jama).c: A rural site near Jama with few amenities: be sure to have the exact coordinates to find it.

thelepte (site archeologique).d: A vast site (~100 ha) located ~5 km north of Feriana (Kasserine). It features mosaic-adorned thermal baths, eleven Christian churches, and a Byzantine citadel.
thelepte (site archeologique).a: A vast area of ruins (~100 ha) featuring thermal baths with mosaics, eleven Christian churches, and a Byzantine citadel.
thelepte (site archeologique).c: About 5 km north of Feriana; this is a large, exposed site, so be sure to bring water and allow plenty of time for the hike.

sufes (sbiba).d: The Roman city of Byzacene (Colonia Aurelia Sufetana), located on the site of present-day Sbiba. A basilica converted into a mosque, a temple, thermal baths, and a Byzantine fortress built by Justinian.
sufes (sbiba).a: The basilica, which was converted into a mosque, the temple, the thermal baths, and Justinian's Byzantine fort, located in what is now Sbiba.
sufes (sbiba).c: Scattered ruins in the modern city: a short visit to combine with Sbeitla.

site archeologique de thala.d: One of the few cities to have retained its ancient name, located at an altitude of ~1,000 m, associated with Jugurtha. Necropolis, two-story mausoleum, Byzantine fortifications.
site archeologique de thala.a: The necropolis, a two-story mausoleum, and Byzantine fortifications, in a rare city that has retained its ancient name linked to Jugurtha.
site archeologique de thala.c: At an altitude of ~1,000 m: be sure to bring warm clothing, as this is one of the coldest places in Tunisia.

mausolee des flavii (cillium).d: A three-story tower mausoleum erected around the middle of the 2nd century near Kasserine, bearing the longest surviving epigraphic poem from the Roman world.
mausolee des flavii (cillium).a: A three-story tower mausoleum dating from the mid-2nd century, bearing the longest surviving epigraphic poem from the Roman world.
mausolee des flavii (cillium).c: The most prominent landmark in the ancient site of Cillium; a quick stop worth making while in Kasserine.

kasbah de beja.d: A citadel overlooking Beja, rebuilt from its Punic and Byzantine origins through the Ottoman period. A cultural center after independence.
kasbah de beja.a: The citadel overlooking Béja, whose ramparts blend Punic, Byzantine, and Ottoman influences; today a cultural center offering a view of the city.
kasbah de beja.c: Hike up from the medina; combine this with a visit to the Great Mosque and the old town of Béja.

grande mosquee de beja.d: The main mosque in the medina of Beja, founded in 944 on the site of an ancient basilica and restored in 1922.
grande mosquee de beja.a: The main mosque in the medina of Béja, founded in 944 on the site of an ancient basilica and restored in 1922.
grande mosquee de beja.c: Appropriate attire is required; discover this as you stroll through the medina of Béja.

pont de medjez el-bab.d: An eight-arch bridge over the Medjerda River, completed in 1677 under Murad II Bey, built using reused Roman stones. Still in use today.
pont de medjez el-bab.a: The eight-arch Ottoman bridge over the Medjerda River, completed in 1677 under Murad II Bey, with its reused Roman stones, is still in use today.
pont de medjez el-bab.c: Visible from the riverbanks; a quick stop along the way, best combined with a visit to the nearby Medjez el-Bab memorial.

fort genois de tabarka.d: A 16th-century Genoese fortress overlooking the old port of Tabarka, a remnant of the Lomellini family’s presence. A lighthouse was added in the late 19th century.
fort genois de tabarka.a: the Genoese fort perched on its small island connected to the coast; the ramparts and the view of the bay and the Aiguilles.
fort genois de tabarka.c: Head up there in the late afternoon to enjoy the view of the famous Aiguilles rocks.

eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.d: A former church built between 1884 and 1891 inside a Roman cistern. No longer used as a place of worship, it now houses a museum; it was designated a historic site in 2016.
eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.a: The former church, converted in the late 19th century from a Roman cistern, is now a museum in the center of Tabarka.
eglise sainte-maxime de tabarka.c: A short visit to include as part of a stroll through town; best combined with a visit to the nearby Genoese fort.

musee national du bardo.d: Tunisia's main museum, housed in a former beylical palace in the Bardo district. It features one of the world's richest collections of Roman mosaics, as well as Punic, early Christian, and Islamic artifacts.
musee national du bardo.a: the world's richest collection of Roman mosaics (Virgil, Odysseus, and the Sirens; Neptune); the Punic galleries and the artifacts from the Mahdia shipwreck.
musee national du bardo.c: Allow two to three hours; this is the highlight of any trip to Tunis.
musee national du bardo.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.
musee national du bardo.an: The Bardo is home to the most beautiful collection of Roman mosaics in the world, housed in a former Beylical palace. Devastated in 2015, it has reopened—a symbol of resilience.

dar hussein.d: An aristocratic palace in the medina of Tunis, featuring a porticoed courtyard, stucco, and marble. It houses the National Heritage Institute.
dar hussein.a: The marble porticoed courtyard, the painted ceilings, the sculpted stucco, and the ceramic tiles of this aristocratic palace, which houses the National Heritage Institute.
dar hussein.c: Access is sometimes restricted because it is an institutional site; worth seeing during a stroll through the lower medina.

dar lasram.d: A spacious patrician mansion in the medina of Tunis, built by the Lasram family. It serves as the headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina (ASM).
dar lasram.a: The grand 18th-century patrician mansion, with its marble courtyard, ornately decorated salons, and driba (vestibule), serves as the headquarters of the Association for the Preservation of the Medina.
dar lasram.c: A fine example of Tunisian patrician architecture; view it alongside the neighboring palaces in the northern quarter of the medina.

mosquee hammouda pacha.d: Hanafi mosque in the Medina of Tunis (early 17th century), with an Ottoman octagonal minaret. It houses the mausoleum of the Mouradite family.
mosquee hammouda pacha.a: the octagonal minaret, inspired by Ottoman architecture; the marble decorations and the courtyard; the mausoleum of the founding bey.
mosquee hammouda pacha.c: Things to see as you stroll through the medina of Tunis.

mosquee de la kasbah.d: The Kasbah Mosque in Tunis, founded in the 13th century under the Hafsids, whose minaret served as a model for Tunisian religious architecture.
mosquee de la kasbah.a: The 13th-century Hafsid minaret, a model of Tunisian religious architecture, overlooks Kasbah Square above the medina.
mosquee de la kasbah.c: Best viewed from the outside, from the square; best visited in combination with the nearby Dar El Bey.

bab saadoun.d: A monumental gate to the northwest of the medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century as a triple arch.
bab saadoun.a: The monumental triple-arched gate, rebuilt in the 19th century, now stands alone at a roundabout northwest of the medina.
bab saadoun.c: Can be viewed from the road; if you are not planning to go inside, plan for a quick stop.

bab jedid.d: A gate in the medina of Tunis, built in the 13th century under the Hafsids, located to the south. A rare medieval gate still standing.
bab jedid.a: The rare medieval Hafsid gate still standing in the southern part of the medina, with its horseshoe arch opening onto the souks.
bab jedid.c: A good starting point for exploring the medina on foot from the south, heading toward Zitouna.

bab el jazira.d: The former southern gate of the Tunis medina, leading toward the road to Kairouan; it has been rebuilt several times.
bab el jazira.a: The old southern gate of the medina, which has been remodeled several times, marks the historic starting point of the road to Kairouan and the entrance to a commercial district.
bab el jazira.c: A lively, working-class neighborhood; a quick visit to round out a stroll through the lower medina.

bab el khadra.d: A gate to the north of the medina of Tunis, rebuilt in the 19th century; its name refers to the gardens beyond the city walls.
bab el khadra.a: The gate, rebuilt in the 19th century on the northern side of the medina, whose name evokes the ancient gardens beyond the ramparts.
bab el khadra.c: A quick, brief stop along the northern edge of the medina.

zaouia de sidi kassim el jelizi.d: A zaouia in the Tunis medina featuring zellij ceramic decorations; the tomb of the saint and potter Sidi Kassim El Jelizi. Ceramics Museum.
zaouia de sidi kassim el jelizi.a: The polychrome ceramic decorations (zellij) that adorn the zaouia, the tomb of the saintly potter, and the collections of the National Ceramics Museum located on the premises.
zaouia de sidi kassim el jelizi.c: A hidden gem of earthenware; ideal for those interested in the decorative arts—a short visit.

mosquee saheb ettabaa.d: A religious complex in the northern part of the medina of Tunis (early 19th century) founded by Youssef Saheb Ettabaa: a mosque, a madrasa, and a mausoleum.
mosquee saheb ettabaa.a: The early 19th-century complex—comprising a mosque, a madrasa, and a mausoleum, decorated with marble and stucco—in the northern part of the medina.
mosquee saheb ettabaa.c: Combine this with a visit to the Saheb Ettabaa Palace and the Halfaouine neighborhood.

cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.d: Tunis Catholic Cathedral (late 19th century) on Habib Bourguiba Avenue, in the Roman-Byzantine composite style. Approximate coordinates.
cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.a: The Roman-Byzantine composite façade overlooking Habib Bourguiba Avenue, and the interior of the capital’s main Catholic church, which is still in use.
cathedrale saint-vincent-de-paul de tuni.c: Right in the heart of the modern city center—a must-see at the beginning or end of a stroll down the avenue.

sidi bou said.d: A village perched above the Gulf of Tunis, famous for its white houses with blue doors. A listed site inspired by Andalusian architecture, located near Carthage.
sidi bou said.a: the Café des Nattes at the top of the main street; the blue doors and mashrabiya screens; Baron d'Erlanger's Ennejma Ezzahra Palace (Museum of Music); the lighthouse and the lookout point overlooking the gulf; the small marina below.
sidi bou said.c: Come in the late afternoon to enjoy the light and the sunset; a pine nut tea at Café des Délices is a must.
sidi bou said.leg: The blue-and-white village owes its name to the Sufi saint Abu Sa'id al-Baji (13th century), whose tomb stands on the hill; sailors used to ask him for protection. The blue-and-white color scheme, however, was imposed much later, in the 20th century, by Baron d’Erlanger.

palais ennejma ezzahra.d: A palace built in Sidi Bou Said by Baron Rodolphe d'Erlanger (early 20th century) in the Arab-Andalusian style. It houses the Center for Arab and Mediterranean Music.
palais ennejma ezzahra.a: the Moorish mansion of Baron d'Erlanger and its terraced gardens; the painted salons; the collection of musical instruments at the Center for Arabic Music.
palais ennejma ezzahra.c: In Sidi Bou Saïd: Combine your visit with a concert or enjoy the view of the gulf from the gardens.

musee national de carthage.d: Archaeological Museum on Byrsa Hill: Punic and Roman collections from the Carthage excavations (stelae, sarcophagi, mosaics).
musee national de carthage.a: the sarcophagi of the Punic priests and priestesses; the stelae of the Tophet; the mosaics and the model of Roman Carthage; the view from Byrsa.
musee national de carthage.c: Visit this site at the start of the Carthage tour to get a sense of where the various sites are located.
musee national de carthage.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.

basilique de damous el karita.d: A vast early Christian basilica in Carthage, one of the largest in North Africa, with numerous naves and an underground rotunda.
basilique de damous el karita.a: The numerous column bases in the multiple naves of one of North Africa’s largest early Christian basilicas, and its underground rotunda.
basilique de damous el karita.c: A quiet area of Carthage; wear sturdy shoes for the grassy terrain and the rotunda.

quartier magon.d: A Punic residential neighborhood in Carthage excavated along the seashore, featuring the remains of dwellings and an open-air museum. Approximate coordinates.
quartier magon.a: The remains of Punic dwellings unearthed along the seashore and the small open-air museum on site that explains the urban layout of Carthage.
quartier magon.c: A short tour along the coast, followed by a visit to the nearby Antoninus Thermal Baths.

villas romaines de carthage (colline de.d: Residential area of Roman Carthage on Odeon Hill, featuring the House of the Aviary with its peristyle and mosaics, and an odeon. Approximate coordinates.
villas romaines de carthage (colline de.a: The Maison de la Volière, with its reconstructed peristyle and original mosaics, its panoramic terraces, and the ruins of the odeon on the hill.
villas romaines de carthage (colline de.c: Beautiful view of Carthage and the sea; should be included in the site's combined ticket.

palais presidentiel de carthage.d: The official residence of the President of the Republic of Tunisia, located on the seafront in Carthage. A 20th-century palatial complex set within an enclosed park.
palais presidentiel de carthage.a: The palace and its enclosed grounds can be glimpsed from the outside; as the official residence of the head of state, the complex is not open to the public.
palais presidentiel de carthage.c: Site not open to the public and under surveillance: do not take photos of the surrounding area; this is simply a landmark along the coastal road.

fort de la goulette (karraka).d: The coastal fortress of La Goulette (Karraka), commanding the entrance to the port of Tunis, was built in the 16th century and was contested by the Spanish and the Ottomans.
fort de la goulette (karraka).a: the 16th-century Ottoman and Spanish fortress guarding the entrance to Lake Tunis; the massive bastions.
fort de la goulette (karraka).c: A must-see when passing through La Goulette, which is famous for its seafood restaurants.

la goulette (halq el oued).d: A port city at the entrance to Lake Tunis, the capital's historic outer harbor. A fishing district with a cosmopolitan atmosphere.
la goulette (halq el oued).a: The waterfront and the harbor, the seafood restaurants along the main avenue, and the traces of the cosmopolitan past (the Italian and Jewish quarters) of Tunis’s former outer harbor.
la goulette (halq el oued).c: Perfect for a grilled fish lunch; accessible by TGM from Tunis.

palais de la rose (manouba).d: A former bey's palace on the Manouba Plain, known as the Palace of the Rose. It houses the National Military Museum of Tunisia.
palais de la rose (manouba).a: The former bey's summer palace and its reception rooms, which today house the National Military Museum, featuring weapons, uniforms, and equipment.
palais de la rose (manouba).c: Of particular interest to military history enthusiasts; check the opening hours before visiting.

zaghouan (ville).d: A mountain town at the foot of Djebel Zaghouan. A Roman nymphaeum (temple of the waters) and an Ottoman medina with ancient fountains.
zaghouan (ville).a: The Ottoman medina with its ancient fountains, the Roman arch, the silhouette of the djebel in the background, and, towering above it all, the Temple of Waters.
zaghouan (ville).c: A pleasant, cool high-altitude base for exploring the Temple of the Waters and Djebel National Park.

hammam lif.d: A seaside and spa resort at the foot of Djebel Boukornine, on the Gulf of Tunis. A former resort favored by the beys, known for its hot springs.
hammam lif.a: The waterfront and the casino—a former royal resort at the foot of Mount Boukornine—the hot springs, and the resort’s old-fashioned seaside atmosphere.
hammam lif.c: Starting point for the hike up to Boukornine National Park, which overlooks the city.

vieux port de bizerte.d: The historic port of Bizerte is lined with old houses and connected to the sea by a channel. It lies at the heart of the medina and was long a base for privateers and fishermen.
vieux port de bizerte.a: The historic harbor, lined with old houses and connected to the sea by a channel, is the picturesque heart of the medina and a former pirate base.
vieux port de bizerte.c: A pleasant stroll along the waterfront in the late afternoon; a great starting point for exploring the kasbah and the medina on foot.

kasbah de bizerte.d: A fortress overlooking the entrance to the old port of Bizerte, with imposing ramparts, protecting the city and its channel.
kasbah de bizerte.a: The fortress with its mighty ramparts guarding the entrance to the old harbor, with its narrow inner streets and views of the channel.
kasbah de bizerte.c: You can walk there from the old port; wear sturdy shoes for the ramparts and narrow alleys.

fort d'espagne (bizerte).d: A fortress on the heights of Bizerte (16th century), built during the Spanish-Ottoman rivalry in the Mediterranean. It overlooks the city and the harbor.
fort d'espagne (bizerte).a: The 16th-century fort perched on the heights of Bizerte, overlooking the city and the harbor, stands as a testament to the Spanish-Ottoman rivalry.
fort d'espagne (bizerte).c: Head up at the end of the day to enjoy the view of the city and the sea; accessible by car or a short walk.

borj loutani (ghar el melh).d: One of the three Ottoman forts at Ghar el Melh (formerly Porto Farina), built in the 17th century to protect the corsair port.
borj loutani (ghar el melh).a: One of the three 17th-century Ottoman forts built to protect the former pirate port of Porto Farina (Ghar el Melh).
borj loutani (ghar el melh).c: Discover this as you tour the three bordjs of Ghar el Melh; combine it with a visit to the lagoon and its Ramli gardens.

borj el woustani (ghar el melh).d: Ghar el Melh Median Fort, an Ottoman fortification defending the former port of Porto Farina on the north coast.
borj el woustani (ghar el melh).a: The central fort at Ghar el Melh, an Ottoman structure defending the ancient port of Porto Farina on the north coast.
borj el woustani (ghar el melh).c: A quick stop between the other two forts at Ghar el Melh; best combined with a visit to the nearby lagoon.

fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).d: A citadel on a 150-meter promontory overlooking the sea and Kelibia, northeast of Cape Bon. It features Roman and Byzantine elements, but most of it dates from a 16th-century reconstruction with Ottoman additions.
fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).a: the fortress overlooking the harbor and the beach; the remodeled Byzantine ramparts; the view of the Cap Bon coastline, stretching all the way to Sicily on a clear day.
fort de kelibia (borj el-kebir).c: An easy hike from the harbor; a stunning view at sunset.

kasbah de hammamet.d: A fortress at the southwest corner of the medina of Hammamet, overlooking the sea. A 9th-century ribat used for coastal surveillance, rebuilt in the 15th century under the Hafsids.
kasbah de hammamet.a: the fort overlooking the old town; the panoramic walkway offering views of the white medina and the beach; the flower-lined alleyways below.
kasbah de hammamet.c: Take a walk along the ramparts at sunset to enjoy the view of the bay.

carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.d: Extensive underground quarries located about 3 km west of El Haouaria, operated from the Punic to the Roman periods; the sandstone was transported by sea to Carthage. Approximate coordinates.
carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.a: the vast underground chambers hewn out of the sandstone from which the stones for Carthage were quarried; the skylights opening out onto the sea.
carrieres romaines de ghar el kebir (el.c: Best enjoyed in combination with the tip of Cap Bon; the galleries offer a pleasant coolness in the summer.

musee de nabeul.d: Nabeul Archaeological Museum (medina), collections from sites in Cap Bon (Neapolis, Kerkouane): mosaics, stelae, and Punic and Roman artifacts.
musee de nabeul.a: An archaeological museum showcasing collections from the Cap Bon sites (Neapolis, Kerkouane): mosaics, stelae, and Punic and Roman artifacts.
musee de nabeul.c: Ideal for planning or extending a visit to Kerkouane and Neapolis.
musee de nabeul.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.

bassins des aghlabides.d: Open-air water reservoirs built around 860 to supply Kairouan, among the major hydraulic structures of the medieval Muslim world; a large circular basin approximately 128 m in diameter.
bassins des aghlabides.a: the two large circular stone basins from the 9th century that supplied Kairouan with water; the lookout point overlooking them.
bassins des aghlabides.c: Go up to the adjacent terrace to get a sense of the geometry of the pools.

mosquee des trois portes.d: Mosque founded in 866 by Muhammad ibn Khairun, in the medina of Kairouan. It features the oldest carved and decorated facade in the Islamic world; a Hafsid minaret was added around 1440.
mosquee des trois portes.a: The 9th-century Aghlabid facade, adorned with carved Kufic inscriptions, is one of the oldest dated mosque facades.
mosquee des trois portes.c: A small monument in the narrow streets of Kairouan, worth seeing as you stroll through the medina.

zaouia de sidi sahbi (mosquee du barbier.d: A zaouia housing the mausoleum of Abu Zamaa al-Balaoui, a companion of the Prophet known as Sidi Sahbi, the patron saint of Kairouan. Rebuilt in the 17th century (madrasa, minaret, Hispano-Moorish decorations).
zaouia de sidi sahbi (mosquee du barbier.a: the courtyards and covered galleries adorned with polychrome earthenware and intricately carved stucco; the mausoleum of a companion of the Prophet.
zaouia de sidi sahbi (mosquee du barbier.c: One of Tunisia's most beautiful ceramic displays; proper attire is required.

medina de kairouan.d: The historic heart of Kairouan, a holy city of Islam founded in 670, surrounded by ramparts and home to the Great Mosque and numerous monuments. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988. Approximate coordinates.
medina de kairouan.a: the Great Mosque; the Aghlabid Pools; the Zaouia of Sidi Sahbi (the Barber's Mosque); the carpet souks; and the Mosque of the Three Gates.
medina de kairouan.c: Buy the combined ticket that grants access to the main monuments; this is a holy city, so modest attire is appreciated.

skifa kahla (bab zouila).d: A monumental fortified gate in the medina of Mahdia, a remnant of the Fatimid ramparts built beginning in 916. It is the only land access point to the historic peninsula.
skifa kahla (bab zouila).a: the monumental fortified gateway, a remnant of the Fatimid ramparts; the long vaulted passageway leading to the medina of Mahdia.
skifa kahla (bab zouila).c: The perfect starting point for exploring the Mahdia Peninsula.

borj el-kebir de mahdia.d: A fort at the tip of the Mahdia Peninsula, built in the 16th century on older foundations. Panoramic view of Cape Africa and the old Fatimid port. Listed as a historic site since 1912.
borj el-kebir de mahdia.a: the square fort overlooking the headland; the terraces opening onto the sea and the nearby maritime cemetery.
borj el-kebir de mahdia.c: Go there at sunset to enjoy the view of Cape Africa.

mausolee de bourguiba (monastir).d: Mausoleum of Habib Bourguiba, the first president of the Tunisian Republic, designed by Olivier-Clement Cacoub. Two minarets and a gilded dome. Approximate coordinates.
mausolee de bourguiba (monastir).a: the mausoleum with its golden dome and minarets; the marble courtyard and the esplanade; the monumental cemetery.
mausolee de bourguiba (monastir).c: Best visited in combination with the nearby ribat; please dress appropriately at this historic site.

mosquee bourguiba de monastir.d: The Great Hanafi Mosque of Monastir, dedicated to Bourguiba, was built in 1963 (architect: Taieb Bouzguenda) and was inspired by the Hammouda Pasha Mosque in Tunis. Approximate coordinates.
mosquee bourguiba de monastir.a: A large Hanafi mosque built in 1963 and inspired by the Hammouda Pasha Mosque in Tunis, located in the medina of Monastir.
mosquee bourguiba de monastir.c: Visits are permitted outside of prayer times; appropriate attire is required.

ribat de lamta.d: A small Aghlabid ribat in Lamta (Leptis Minor), built in 859. It is a square, single-story building with rounded corner towers and a courtyard featuring an underground cistern.
ribat de lamta.a: Small Aghlabid ribat dating from 859 in Lamta (Leptis Minor): a single-story square building with rounded corner towers and a courtyard featuring an underground cistern.
ribat de lamta.c: Combine this with a visit to the nearby Lamta Archaeological Museum.

musee archeologique de lamta.d: The museum opened in 1992 on the seashore at ancient Leptiminus. Its collections span the period from the arrival of the Phoenicians through the Roman and early Christian eras.
musee archeologique de lamta.a: A seaside museum located on the site of ancient Leptiminus, tracing the local history from the Phoenicians through the Roman and Early Christian periods.
musee archeologique de lamta.c: Combine this visit with a trip to the nearby Lamta Ribat.
musee archeologique de lamta.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.

leptiminus (leptis minor).d: An ancient city corresponding to present-day Lamta, founded around 500 B.C. The center of a prosperous Roman olive-growing district: Punic tombs, an amphitheater, thermal baths, and aqueducts. Approximate coordinates.
leptiminus (leptis minor).a: the ruins of the ancient port and thermal baths; the small museum displaying local ceramics and mosaics.
leptiminus (leptis minor).c: A quiet site in Lamta, perfect for archaeology enthusiasts, best visited in combination with the nearby ribat.

koubba de sidi el mezri (monastir).d: Shrine and koubba of the saint Sidi Mezri (died in 1141), located within the large seaside cemetery of Sidi El Mezri near the ribat. Approximate coordinates.
koubba de sidi el mezri (monastir).a: The shrine and koubba of the saint Sidi Mezri (who died in 1141), located in the heart of the large seaside cemetery of the same name, near the ribat.
koubba de sidi el mezri (monastir).c: Worth seeing on your way from the ribat to Bourguiba's mausoleum.

kasbah de sousse (tour du khalef).d: A fortress located at the highest point of the medina of Sousse, incorporated into the city walls in the 11th century, and encompassing the Khalef Tower (859). It houses the archaeological museum.
kasbah de sousse (tour du khalef).a: A fortress at the highest point of the medina, incorporating the Khalef Tower (859) and housing the archaeological museum, which features a rich collection of mosaics.
kasbah de sousse (tour du khalef).c: Combine a visit to the kasbah and its museum; the highest point offers a beautiful view of the medina.

musee archeologique d'el jem (maison d'a.d: Museum near the amphitheater at El Jem (Thysdrus), featuring a significant collection of mosaics. Park with Roman villas, including the reconstructed House of Africa.
musee archeologique d'el jem (maison d'a.a: An extensive collection of mosaics near the amphitheater, along with a complex of Roman villas, including the reconstructed House of Africa.
musee archeologique d'el jem (maison d'a.c: Next, head to the nearby amphitheater to learn about ancient Thysdrus.
musee archeologique d'el jem (maison d'a.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.

thapsus (ras dimass, bekalta).d: An ancient Carthaginian and later Roman port city located at a place called Ras Dimass (Bekalta, Monastir). Punic, Roman, and medieval ruins are threatened by urbanization and erosion.
thapsus (ras dimass, bekalta).a: the ruins of the Roman port and submerged breakwaters; the site of the battle where Caesar defeated the Pompeians in 46 B.C.
thapsus (ras dimass, bekalta).c: A scattered coastal site; of primarily historical interest.

bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).d: Decisive battle in which Julius Caesar defeated the Pompeians led by Metellus Scipio and King Juba I near Thapsus, putting an end to the conflict in Africa. Presumed, approximate location.
bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).a: Presumed site of the battle in which Caesar defeated the Pompeians and Juba I; there are no specific ruins, only the coastal landscape of Thapsus.
bataille de thapsus (46 av. j.-c.).c: More of a historical landmark than a tourist site; best viewed in conjunction with the ruins of Thapsus.

acholla (botria).d: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, near Botria. It features some of the oldest Romano-African mosaics in Tunisia (at the Bardo), a forum, two thermal baths, and houses.
acholla (botria).a: A Punic and later Roman city on the Sahel coast, known for some of the oldest mosaics in Tunisia (now at the Bardo Museum), a forum, two thermal baths, and residential houses.
acholla (botria).c: The most beautiful mosaics are at the Bardo Museum; once there, be sure to hire a guide to help you interpret the artifacts.

pheradi maius (sidi khalifa).d: A Roman city in Proconsular Africa near Sidi Khalifa, north of Enfidha. Temples, thermal baths, a triumphal arch, a forum, and an amphitheater.
pheradi maius (sidi khalifa).a: A well-preserved Roman site near Sidi Khalifa: temples, thermal baths, a triumphal arch, a forum, and the remains of an amphitheater.
pheradi maius (sidi khalifa).c: An outdoor site off the beaten path; check with locals for directions.

uzita (henchir makhrba).d: Ancient city and episcopal see of Byzacene (Henchir el-Makrceba, Monastir), near the sebkhas of Sidi El Hani and Sahline. Of Phoenician origin, with mosaics.
uzita (henchir makhrba).a: An ancient city of Phoenician origin and the episcopal see of Byzacène, known for its mosaics, located near the sebkhas of Sidi El Hani and Sahline.
uzita (henchir makhrba).c: A modest and little-known archaeological site; of interest mainly to lovers of antiquity.

medina de sfax.d: The historic center of Sfax, founded by the Aghlabids around 849–851, is one of the few medieval cities in the Maghreb to have preserved its urban layout and city walls. UNESCO Tentative List.
medina de sfax.a: the medieval ramparts and Bab Diwan; the covered souks, which are still very lively; the Great Mosque; the kasbah; and the Heritage Museum.
medina de sfax.c: One of the most authentic medinas, with few tourists; enter through Bab Diwan and follow the artisan souks.

bab diwan (sfax).d: The main gate of the Sfax medina, located on the southern side of the city walls. Until the 20th century, the medina had only two entrances: Bab Diwan and Bab Jebli.
bab diwan (sfax).a: The main gate of the medina, located on the southern side of the city walls; for a long time, it was one of only two entrances to the city.
bab diwan (sfax).c: The perfect starting point for a walking tour of the medina.

bab jebli (sfax).d: The second historic gate of the Sfax medina, located on the northern side of the city walls.
bab jebli (sfax).a: The second historic gate of the medina, located on the northern side of the ramparts, leading to the food souks.
bab jebli (sfax).c: The more popular North Coast: a great starting point for everyday activities.

kasbah de sfax.d: A fortress at the southwest corner of the Sfax medina, integrated into the ramparts and commanding the defense of this sector. Approximate coordinates.
kasbah de sfax.a: A fortress at the southwest corner of the medina, built into the city walls; it now houses a museum.
kasbah de sfax.c: Climb up to the ramparts for a panoramic view of the medina.

borj el ksar (sfax).d: A fortification at the northwest corner of the medina of Sfax (11th–12th centuries), featuring three towers. It houses a collection of stone carvings.
borj el ksar (sfax).a: An 11th- to 12th-century corner fortification with three towers, housing a collection of stone carvings.
borj el ksar (sfax).c: Combine this with a walk along the medina's ramparts.

henchir-khachoum (muzuca).d: A group of sites in the governorate of Sidi Bouzid, identified with the ancient city of Muzuca, a Roman civitas and the seat of a bishopric attached to Carthage.
henchir-khachoum (muzuca).a: The scattered ruins of ancient Muzuca, a Roman civitas and former episcopal see.
henchir-khachoum (muzuca).c: A modest, largely undeveloped rural site: most useful to archaeology enthusiasts with precise coordinates.

musee archeologique de gafsa.d: The Gafsa Medina Museum, which houses a rich collection of Capsian stone and bone tools, as well as Roman artifacts and mosaics from ancient Capsa. Approximate coordinates.
musee archeologique de gafsa.a: Collections of Capsian tools (stone and bone), Roman artifacts, and mosaics from ancient Capsa.
musee archeologique de gafsa.c: A pleasant stop with air conditioning during the hottest part of the day; check the schedule on site.
musee archeologique de gafsa.h: Museum — open during the day (may be closed one day a week); check opening hours on site.
